query_text: Why does my cat kick its toys when playing with them?

message.content:
Your cat's kicking behavior, often called "bunny kicking," is completely natural and stems from deep-rooted instincts. Here are the main reasons why cats kick their toys:

## Hunting Instinct

The primary reason cats bunny kick is that they're practicing their **predatory skills**. In the wild, cats use this powerful hind leg motion to subdue or disembowel prey. Even well-fed house cats retain these hunting instincts, and toys trigger the same behaviors they'd use on real prey. Kittens actually learn this behavior early through play with their mothers and littermates.

## Play Fighting Practice

Bunny kicking serves as **practice for real confrontations**. When cats playfully wrestle with each other, you'll often see them roll on their backs, grab their "opponent" with their front paws, and kick vigorously with their hind legs. This helps them develop coordination and keep their fighting skills sharp in a safe context.

## Defensive Behavior

The kicking motion is also a **defensive maneuver**. When a cat rolls onto its back, it can use all four sets of claws plus its teeth to protect itself. This position allows them to defend their vulnerable belly while still being able to inflict maximum damage on a threat. Your cat is essentially keeping these survival skills honed even when just playing with a stuffed toy.

## Physical and Mental Benefits

Bunny kicking provides excellent **full-body exercise** that engages core muscles, hind leg strength, and cardiovascular health. It also offers mental stimulation and stress relief—completing the "capture and kill" sequence with a toy releases endorphins and satisfies their natural drive.

## When to Be Cautious

While kicking toys is normal, watch for signs that play has turned aggressive: pinned-back ears, hissing, puffed-up fur, stiff posture, or rapidly swishing tail. If your cat redirects kicking at you, simply stop the interaction and offer an appropriate kicker toy instead.
